members.local_label: Section 2.2 — GMDD, the two displayed expressions
members.source_heading: Section 2.2 — GMDD, the two displayed expressions
members.statement_original:
Given a Lévy measure $\mu$, GMDD of $U$ given $V$ is defined as
\[
\operatorname{GMDD}(U\mid V)=\int_{\mathbb R^p}\|g_{U,V}(s)-g_Ug_V(s)\|_2^2\mu(ds),
\]
where $g_{U,V}(s)=E(Ue^{is^\top V})$, $g_U=E(U)$, $g_V(s)=E(e^{is^\top V})$ and $\|\cdot\|_2$ represents $l_2$ norm of complex-valued vector space $\mathbb C^q$.

\[
\operatorname{GMDD}(U\mid V)=-E\{(U-EU)^\top(\widetilde U-E\widetilde U)\kappa(V,\widetilde V)\},
\]
where $(\widetilde U,\widetilde V)$ is an independent copy of $(U,V)$.

members.local_label: Section 3.1 — nonlinear SDR problem (5)
members.source_heading: Section 3.1 — nonlinear SDR problem (5)
members.statement_original:
Consider the following nonlinear SDR problem
\[
Y\mathrel{\perp\!\!\!\perp}X\mid\boldsymbol f^0(X),\tag{5}
\]
where $\boldsymbol f^0(\cdot)$ is a $\mathbb R^d$-valued function $(d\le p)$. That is to say, at least $d$ functions of $p$-dimensional $X$ are needed to fully capture the relationship between $Y$ and $X$. The intrinsic dimension $d$ is assumed known for simplicity. Obviously, $\boldsymbol f^0$ is unidentifiable since we can replace $\boldsymbol f^0(X)$ by any one-to-one function of it without affecting the conditional independence (5).

evidence.location: Section 3.1 — nonlinear SDR problem (5)

members.local_label: Assumption — dominated conditional distributions and central σ-field
members.source_heading: Assumption — dominated conditional distributions and central σ-field
members.statement_original:
Assume that the family of probability measures $\{P_{X\mid Y}(\cdot\mid y):y\in\Omega\}$ is dominated by a σ-finite measure. Then there exists a unique minimal sufficient σ-field (or central σ-field) $\mathscr G_{Y\mid X}$ such that
\[
Y\mathrel{\perp\!\!\!\perp}X\mid\mathscr G_{Y\mid X}.
\]
Moreover, $\boldsymbol f^0$ in (5) satisfies $E\{\boldsymbol f^0(X)\}=0$, $\operatorname{Var}\{\boldsymbol f^0(X)\}=I_d$ and
\[
\sigma\{\boldsymbol f^0(X)\}=\mathscr G_{Y\mid X}.
\]

evidence.location: Assumption — dominated conditional distributions and central σ-field

members.local_label: Section 3.1 — central class
members.source_heading: Section 3.1 — central class
members.statement_original: Following [27], let $\mathfrak M_{\sigma\{\boldsymbol f^0(X)\}}$ be the central class corresponding to the central σ-field $\sigma\{\boldsymbol f^0(X)\}$, which is the set of all square-integrable, $\sigma\{\boldsymbol f^0(X)\}$-measurable functions. Equivalently, $\mathfrak M_{\sigma\{\boldsymbol f^0(X)\}}$ is a subset of $L_2(P_X)$ and it consists of all elements that can be expressed as functions of $\boldsymbol f^0$.

evidence.location: Section 3.1 — central class

members.local_label: Theorem 3.2 — optimal solution and ordered GMDD values
members.source_heading: Theorem 3.2 — optimal solution and ordered GMDD values
members.statement_original:
Let $m$ be any positive integer no greater than the dimension of $\mathfrak M_{\sigma\{\boldsymbol f^0(X)\}}$, which can be infinite. If $\boldsymbol f^*$ is an optimal solution of the following objective function
\[
\begin{aligned}
\max_{\boldsymbol f\in\{L_2(P_X)\}^m}\;&-E\big([\boldsymbol f(X)-E\{\boldsymbol f(X)\}]^\top[\boldsymbol f(\widetilde X)-E\{\boldsymbol f(\widetilde X)\}]\kappa(Y,\widetilde Y)\big)\\
\text{subject to}\;&\operatorname{Var}\{\boldsymbol f(X)\}=I_m,
\end{aligned}\tag{6}
\]
then $f_j^*\in\mathfrak M_{\sigma\{\boldsymbol f^0(X)\}}$ for all $1\le j\le m$. By Lemma 1 in [26], the GMDD matrix
\[
-E\big([\boldsymbol f^*(X)-E\{\boldsymbol f^*(X)\}][\boldsymbol f^*(\widetilde X)-E\{\boldsymbol f^*(\widetilde X)\}]^\top\kappa(Y,\widetilde Y)\big)
\]
is positive semidefinite and thus diagonalizable via an orthogonal matrix. Thereafter, unless otherwise emphasized, we always select $\boldsymbol f^*$ to diagonalize the GMDD matrix and rearrange $f_j^*$ such that its negative GMDD value is nondecreasing. That is to say, for $1\le i<j\le m$,
\[
\lambda_i^*=E\{\bar f_i^*(X)\bar f_i^*(\widetilde X)\kappa(Y,\widetilde Y)\}\le E\{\bar f_j^*(X)\bar f_j^*(\widetilde X)\kappa(Y,\widetilde Y)\}=\lambda_j^*\le0,
\]
where $\bar f_i^*(X)=f_i^*(X)-E\{f_i^*(X)\}$.

evidence.location: Theorem 3.2 — optimal solution and ordered GMDD values

members.local_label: Section 3.2 — penalized population objectives and minimizers (8)–(9)
members.source_heading: Section 3.2 — penalized population objectives and minimizers (8)–(9)
members.statement_original:
Let $\boldsymbol\mu=(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_d)$ with $\mu_j>0$, $1\le j\le d$, be the hyper-parameter vector. First, consider
\[
L_1(\mu_1,f_1)=E\big([f_1(X)-E\{f_1(X)\}][f_1(\widetilde X)-E\{f_1(\widetilde X)\}]\kappa(Y,\widetilde Y)\big)+\mu_1[\operatorname{Var}\{f_1(X)\}-1]^2,
\]
and its corresponding minimizer
\[
f^*_{1,\mu_1}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{f_1\in L_2(P_X)}L_1(\mu_1,f_1).
\]
For $2\le j\le d$, consider
\[
\begin{aligned}
L_j(\mu_j,(\boldsymbol f^*_{[j-1]},f_j))={}&E\big([f_j(X)-E\{f_j(X)\}][f_j(\widetilde X)-E\{f_j(\widetilde X)\}]\kappa(Y,\widetilde Y)\big)\\
&+\mu_j[\operatorname{Var}\{f_j(X)\}-1]^2+\tilde\mu\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}\{\operatorname{Cov}(f^*_{i,\mu_i}(X),f_j(X))\}^2,
\end{aligned}\tag{8}
\]
where $\boldsymbol f^*_{[j-1]}=(f^*_{1,\mu_1},\ldots,f^*_{j-1,\mu_{j-1}})$ and $\tilde\mu>0$ is a predefined constant. Then its corresponding minimizer is
\[
f^*_{j,\mu_j}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{f_j\in L_2(P_X)}L_j(\mu_j,(\boldsymbol f^*_{[j-1]},f_j)).\tag{9}
\]
We refer to the above procedure as the successive direction extraction method.

members.local_label: Section 2.1 — covering number
members.source_heading: Section 2.1 — covering number
members.statement_original:
A finite colloction $f_1,\ldots,f_m:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R$ is called a $\epsilon$-covering of $\mathcal F_n$ with the $L_2(Q)$ norm if for any $f\in\mathcal F_n$ there exists $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ such that $\|f-f_i\|_{L_2(Q)}\le\epsilon$. The corresponding $\epsilon$-covering number of $\mathcal F_n$ is defined as
\[
N(\epsilon,\mathcal F_n,\|\cdot\|_{L_2(Q)}):=\inf\{m\in\mathbb N:\exists\text{a }\varepsilon\text{-cover }f_1,\ldots,f_m\text{ of }\mathcal F_n\}.
\]

members.local_label: Section 2.3 — ReLU feedforward network and architecture sizes
members.source_heading: Section 2.3 — ReLU feedforward network and architecture sizes
members.statement_original:
Specifically, the feedforward neural network can be expressed by
\[
f(x)=W_{\mathcal L}\circ\sigma\circW_{\mathcal L-1}\circ\sigma\circ\cdots\circ\sigma\circW_1\circ\sigma\circW_0(x),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^p,
\]
where $W_i(x)=\omega_i x+b_i$ is an affine transformation with the weight matrix $\omega_i\in\mathbb R^{k_{i+1}\times k_i}$ and intercept vector $b_i\in\mathbb R^{k_{i+1}}$, $i=0,1,\ldots,\mathcal L$, and $\sigma(a)=\max\{a,0\}$ is the ReLU activation function applied element-wise. Here $k_0$ and $k_{\mathcal L+1}$ are the input and output dimensions, respectively. And $k_i$, $i=1,2,\ldots,\mathcal L$ is the number of neurons (width) in the $i$th hidden layer.

The depth of a network is defined as the number $\mathcal L$ of hidden layers, and its width refers to the maximum width $\mathcal N=\max\{k_1,k_2,\ldots,k_{\mathcal L}\}$ of hidden layers. The size of a network can be further measured by two more quantities: the total number of neurons $\mathcal U=\sum_{i=1}^{\mathcal L}k_i$, and the total number of parameters $\mathcal S=\sum_{i=0}^{\mathcal L}k_{i+1}\cdot(k_i+1)$.

evidence.location: Section 2.3 — ReLU feedforward network and architecture sizes

members.local_label: Section 2.1 — Hölder class
members.source_heading: Section 2.1 — Hölder class
members.statement_original:
The function $f:[0,1]^p\to\mathbb R$ is β-Hölder continuous if there exist $\beta\in(0,1]$ and $\zeta>0$ such that
\[
|f(x_1)-f(x_2)|\le\zeta\|x_1-x_2\|_2^\beta\qquad\text{for any }x_1,x_2\in[0,1]^p.
\]
The β-Hölder continuous function class is denoted by $C^\beta([0,1]^p)$.

members.local_label: Section 4 — directionwise and total excess risk
members.source_heading: Section 4 — directionwise and total excess risk
members.statement_original:
We define the excess risk for the $j$th step estimation
\[
R_j(\mu_j,\hat f_{j,\mu_j})=L_j(\mu_j,(\boldsymbol f^*_{[j-1]},\hat f_{j,\mu_j}))-L_j(\mu_j,(\boldsymbol f^*_{[j-1]},f^*_{j,\mu_j}))
\]
and the total excess risk
\[
R(\boldsymbol\mu,\hat{\boldsymbol f})=\sum_{j=1}^dR_j(\mu_j,\hat f_{j,\mu_j}),
\]
where $\boldsymbol\mu=(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_d)$, $\hat{\boldsymbol f}=\hat{\boldsymbol f}_{[d]}=(\hat f_{1,\mu_1},\ldots,\hat f_{d,\mu_d})$ and $\boldsymbol f^*_{[j-1]}=(f^*_{1,\mu_1},\ldots,f^*_{j-1,\mu_{j-1}})$.
